name: Basare / Bassari
catalog_citation: Pike, Kenneth L. 1966. Tagmemic and Matrix Linguistics Applied to Selected African Languages. Final Report, U.S. Office of Education, Bureau of Research (ERIC ED010547). Ch. VI, section 6.1 'Quasi-Isochronic Units of an Accentual Hierarchy', pp. 125-131 (Basa…
catalog_locator: Pike 1966 pp. 125 and 128-129 (PDF pages 132, 135-136; page images the copy we hold, the latter two rendered during this reading from the copy we hold); Dakub…
catalog_quote: In Basare, work in collaboration with Monica Cox led to the postulation of quasi-isochronic feet which were in some sense simultaneously accentual units, and an accentual hierarchy which interlocked with the grammatical hierarchy but was not identical with it. ... The stressed syllables (which I shall now call "accented syllables" in order to avoid the implication of intensity in the term "stress") remained the same in number. ... [1] ā "ñí |t·ú'wān| tùm-mí-nēē 'You know |thing| which-is-here' ... [4] ā "dákáfí |t·ú'wān| tùm-mí-nēē 'You taste |thing| which-is-here' ... Junctures precede the unaccented syllables. [p. 128:] Within a foot, furthermore, the spoken syllables, when measured, reveal a definite pattern of long syllables occurring as the nuclei of feet, and short syllables as prenuclear. ... There seem to be contrasts between a foot with stress on the first syllable with a foot …

new_statements.quote: Nor is the problem of stress synonymous with the problem of speech rhythm. In Bassari, every word has an accented syllable (Cox 1974: 25), and it has been shown that the occurrence of the accent marks approximately isochronous metrical feet (Pike 1966). Phonetically this accent is marked by relative length and a non-centralized allophone of the vowel, and its location is grammatically determined. Differences of intensity occur in speech, but Cox (1974: 26) does not indicate what might govern them.
new_statements.citation: Kropp Dakubu, M. E. 1981. On the characterization of stress in West African tone languages. Afrika und Übersee 64: 227-236, at p. 235 (reporting Cox, Monica. 1974. La phonologie du bassari. Lomé: INRS, pp. 25-26); corroborating first-hand transcriptions in Pike 1966: 125-131.
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Quote check: the Dakubu 1981 passage is present verbatim (string-identical) in at the [p.235] locator, and the underlying Google Books search-within-volume JSON (id -TEzAAAAIAAJ) contains six independently retrieved, mutually overlapping p.235 snippets ('not claimed', 'In Bassari', 'every word', 'metrical feet', 'non-centralized', 'Pike 1966') that tile the whole sentence chain without gaps, plus the p.236 reference-list snippet 'Cox, Monica, 1974: La Phonologie du Bassari; Institut National de la Recherche Scientifique, Lome (Togo)'. So the stitched text is trustworthy, but it remains snippet custody of a second-hand report (Dakubu summarising Cox 1974: 25-26); I could not re-verify agains…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Ntcham is a three-tone language that also has one accented syllable per word; the accent is cued by vowel length and full (non-centralized) vowel quality rather than intensity, and its position is fixed by morphological/grammatical structure rather than by a syllable count. In Pike's (1966) first-hand Basare transcriptions the accent consistently falls on the first syllable of the root: word-initial in prefixless verbs ('bátí, 'dákáfí), after the noun-class prefix in nouns (t·ú'wān 'thing', bī'nìb 'people'). The 'root-initial' reading is my inference from 'grammatically determined' plus those transcriptions; no opened source states the position rule in words.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing stated. Pike 1966 describes a hierarchy of feet grouping into phonological phrases/clauses with an early pitch-marked nucleus, i.e. phrase-level prominence above the word accent, not secondary word stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None in the accessible text. Pike notes utterance-final syllables are lengthened regardless of accent (pre-pausal cue), and that amplitude does not correlate with perceived accent.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level accent ('every word has an accented syllable'), described alongside a separate three-level lexical tone system (Westermann 1922; Cox 1982 apud Adouna 2014; Gblem-Poidi 2016; Hartell 1993). Pike's evidence is from clause-length utterances (isochronous feet), not citation forms. Statement is second-hand (Dakubu summarizing Cox 1974) and was read only through Google Books snippets.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources refer to the same language, Ntcham ntch1242 (ISO bud), under the names Tobote (Westermann 1922, Bassar town speaker recorded 1907), Basari/Basare (Abbott & Cox 1966, Pike 1966: GILLBT fieldwork on the Ghana side), Bassari (Cox 1974, Dakubu 1981), ncàm/n'cam (Takassi: Kabou dialect; Podi: Bassar-ville and Linangmanli of Bapuré; Gblem-Poidi: mpeetɩ́m and ntàapʋ́m varieties). Not to be confused with Basari/Oniyan of Senegal-Guinea (Tenda, ISO bsc) — the JWAL 8.2 'phrase basari' article (Ferry 1971) is that language and was discarded.

sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: First-hand but phrase-rhythm oriented: Basare has 'accented syllables' (Pike avoids 'stress' to avoid implying intensity) heading quasi-isochronous feet; accented syllables measure long, the pre-accent syllable especially short; amplitude does not track perceived accent; 'junctures precede the unaccented syllables'. No explicit rule for position in the word, but every transcribed accent sits on the root-initial syllable: prefixless verbs 'ní, 'bátí, 'cáá, 'dákáfí, 'gífí-bì, 'káá; nouns after the class prefix t·ú'wān 'thing', bī'nìb 'people'.
